findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. Someone who reads only this paragraph can already say what the project is and why it matters.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. … It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The title and heading are about firstmate, a project the newcomer has probably never heard of, and not about Athena. Someone arriving at Athena's home URL has to read the lede before learning that this page is a sample of Athena's output.
findings.source:
/

Athena explains how firstmate handles work

findings.text: The demonstration shows a side capability (reading and explaining a project). It does not show the main promise from the lede: a commit traced to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict. A newcomer sees no example of that commit trail.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: clone, install, then a first command, with a short description of what happens when you press Enter. A link near the top jumps straight to them, so the reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps": "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git", "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The prerequisites leave gaps. The page never says which operating systems are supported or whether a Rust toolchain is needed. It also doesn't say what account or paid access Claude Code needs. The lede mentions "a different one" checking the work, but the page doesn't say which second model or provider that is.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)."

findings.text: This link sits in the header and speaks to an "owner" the newcomer is not. Nothing on the page says who the owner is or what the proposals are, so a first-time reader gets nothing from it.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of firstmate's scripts, with exit codes, locks and pending-close records. A newcomer to Athena will likely skim or leave here. It works as evidence of rigour but not as onboarding.
The page openly says the study is based only on reading the code, with nothing run. This helps trust: a newcomer can see where the page's claims stop.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": "every claim is marked read" … "none was run, so no run confirmed that a script behaves as its header says."

findings.text: This guide sentence is awkward, and the definitions it points to come right after it, not "below the cards' heading". It is a minor wording problem in a section that is already dense.
findings.source: "The two deciders are explained below the cards' heading."

findings.text: This mentions an internal studies/ folder without a link or saying which repository it is in. To a newcomer it is a dead end.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
